title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
The page has two parts.

(1) It ends the Scholium of §38 on case IV, a beam with both ends simply supported (pinned).
- Earlier Euler showed that every root is exact, ω = nπ, so the frequencies go as n², i.e. 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …
- In contrast, the string's partials go as 1, 2, 3, 4, ….
- The second mode is exactly two octaves above the fundamental (ratio 4).
- The third (ratio 9) lies more than three octaves up (9 > 8). Euler argues it is too shrill to be heard.
- So effectively only the fundamental and its double octave sound together. He concludes that such a rod gives 'much purer' tones than simple strings and should have a peculiar sweetness in music.

(2) It begins case V, a beam simply supported at E (s = 0) and clamped ('as if firmly fixed into a wall') at F (s = a).
- Euler uses the Euler–Bernoulli separated solution y(s) = α e^{s/f} + β e^{-s/f} + γ sin(s/f) + δ cos(s/f).
- At the pinned end, y = 0 and y'' = 0 give β = −α and δ = 0, exactly as in case IV.
- At the clamped end, y(a) = 0 and y'(a) = 0. With ω = a/f these read:
  - α e^ω + β e^{−ω} + γ sin ω + δ cos ω = 0,
  - α e^ω − β e^{−ω} + γ cos ω − δ sin ω = 0.
- Substituting gives α(e^ω − e^{−ω}) + γ sin ω = 0 and α(e^ω + e^{−ω}) + γ cos ω = 0.

On the next page Euler eliminates α/γ to get the frequency equation tan ω = tanh ω. This is the standard clamped–pinned characteristic equation; Euler notes it coincides with that of his case II. The mode shape is proportional to sinh(uω) − (sinh ω / sin ω) sin(uω), with u = s/a, and the frequency is ∝ ω²/a².
errors: No mathematical errors: the boundary conditions, the substitutions and the resulting linear system are correct.

The acoustic claim is a judgement rather than an error. Saying the ratio-9 partial is 'scarcely ever heard' because of its pitch is a perceptual assumption. In reality the audibility of higher beam modes depends on how the rod is excited and on damping.

ideas.what: Pinned–pinned beam has overtone series proportional to n², so the partials are 1, double octave, then 9 (beyond three octaves). Euler compares this with the string's harmonic series and calls the rod's tone purer.
ideas.modern_name: Eigenfrequencies of the simply supported Euler–Bernoulli beam, ω_n ∝ n²π²
ideas.usually_credited_to: Daniel Bernoulli and Euler (1735–1744); the musical comparison is discussed in Truesdell 1960
ideas.where_published: E526 itself; related material in E65 (Additamentum de curvis elasticis, 1744) and Euler's correspondence with D. Bernoulli

ideas.what: Clamped–pinned beam: setting up the boundary conditions that lead to tan ω = tanh ω.
ideas.modern_name: Characteristic equation of the clamped–pinned (propped cantilever) beam
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E526); also treated in Rayleigh's Theory of Sound
ideas.where_published: E526, §39ff; Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II 11/2)

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard boundary-value computations for the Euler–Bernoulli beam, plus a musical remark already discussed in Truesdell's history. Nothing on the page appears absent from the literature.
